summary: This unit teaches you to tint eyelashes and eyebrows, shape eyebrows and apply false lashes safely. You will learn to consult and check for contraindications around the eyes, carry out and read a skin test, handle tints and developer safely, measure and design a brow shape, tweeze, thread and wax brows, apply and remove strip and individual lashes, deal with contra-actions, give aftercare advice and keep records.

blocks.p: Lash and brow treatments are small, quick services that make a big difference to a client's face. They are also treatments right next to the **eye**, one of the most delicate parts of the body. This unit, for COSMETOLOGY LEVEL 2 trainees, teaches you to tint lashes and brows, shape brows and apply false lashes, with the eye's safety first every time.

A tint that runs into the eye, a tint used without a skin test, dirty tweezers, or a strip lash pulled off roughly can injure the eye, cause a serious allergic reaction, spread an infection or pull out the client's own lashes. So this unit is about **checking, testing, hygiene and care** as much as about shaping and colour.

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays) and two practical tasks. In one you carry out a skin test, then a lash and brow tint. In the other you measure and shape brows with tweezers, and apply and remove strip lashes. The assessor watches the skin test record, your checks, safety, hygiene, timing, finish and aftercare, not only the result.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: In practical work, take close-ups of the eye or brow area only. Take a whole-face photo only if the client agrees in writing and the Centre allows it.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: The eye, the hair and the products

ul: The skin around the eye is the thinnest on the body, so it stains, swells and reacts easily.
The eyelids protect the eye and spread tears across it. The lashes grow from follicles along the lid edges and keep dust out.

The **conjunctiva** is the thin membrane over the white of the eye and the inside of the lids. When it is infected or irritated it goes red, waters and feels gritty: **conjunctivitis** ('pink eye'), which spreads very easily.
A **stye** is an infected lash follicle or gland at the lid edge: a red, painful lump.

head: Stage
What happens
Why it matters
rows: Anagen (growing)
The hair is attached to its blood supply at the base of the **follicle** and grows.
Lash and brow hairs have a short anagen, so they stay short.
Catagen (changing)
A short stage: the hair stops growing and comes away from its blood supply.
It is brief, so you rarely see it, but it is the step between growing and resting.
Telogen (resting)
The hair rests, then falls out as a new one pushes up.
Lashes shed and regrow over about 6 to 8 weeks, so a tint 'lasts' about 4 to 6 weeks as tinted lashes fall out. Tweezed brow hairs grow back in about 4 to 6 weeks.

blocks.p: Each lash and brow hair is at a different stage, so a few shed every day. Pulling out brow hairs does not stop them growing back, though very frequent plucking over years can thin them.

head: Product
What it is
Key points
rows: Lash and brow tint
A permanent dye made for the eye area, in black, blue-black, brown, light brown and grey.
Never use hair colour made for the head: it is far stronger and can seriously injure the eye.
Developer
A weak **hydrogen peroxide** (often 3%, or '10 volume') liquid or cream.
It starts the chemical reaction that develops the colour in the tint. Use only the strength the tint maker says.
Barrier cream (petroleum jelly)
Protects the skin around the eye from staining.
Keep it off the lashes: tint cannot take through it.
Protective eye shields or damp pads
Paper shields or shaped cotton pads placed under the lower lashes.
Catch tint and keep it off the skin and out of the eye.
Tint stain remover
Lifts tint from the skin.
Away from the eyes only.

head: Client
Lashes
Brows
rows: Dark hair, deep skin tone
Black or blue-black
Black or dark brown; black can look harsh, so brown is often softer
Brown hair
Black or dark brown
Brown, a shade close to the hair
Fair, red or grey hair; pale skin
Brown or dark brown
Light brown or grey; never black

blocks.note: Lashes can take the darkest colour: they look longer and thicker. Brows are usually tinted one shade close to the hair colour, or a little darker. Colours can be mixed from the same maker's range; leave the tint on for less time for a lighter result.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: Read the maker's instructions and follow them every time; do not mix brands.
Mix only what you need, just before use, in a clean **non-metallic** dish (metal can react with the peroxide). Measure carefully. Throw away any leftover: mixed tint cannot be kept.
Wear gloves if the maker or the Centre says so, and work in a ventilated room.

Keep lids on tightly. Store tints and developer in a cool, dark, dry place, in their labelled containers, away from heat and sunlight, out of reach of children. Hydrogen peroxide breaks down in light and heat and loses its strength, and it is kept away from anything that burns.
Check expiry dates and use the oldest stock first.
Know where the sterile **eye wash** and the first aid kit are.

blocks.note: Tint and developer bottles do not like Jamaican heat. A hot shelf by a window or a wax heater spoils them: the developer goes weak and the tint will not take. Keep them in a cool cupboard.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Consultation, contraindications and the skin test

blocks.p: Sit the client in good light, explain the treatment, and fill in the record card with her. She signs it before you start.

head: Ask about
Why it matters
rows: Allergies: to tint, hair dye, lash adhesive, latex, plasters, nickel (metal tools)
A reaction next to the eye can be serious. Dye allergy can appear at any time, even after years of safe use.
Past reactions to any eye treatment
Shapes your choice of products or stops the treatment.
Eye problems, recent eye surgery or laser treatment, eye infections
No treatment near the eye until a doctor says it is safe.
Contact lenses
She must take them out before a tint: tint or water could get behind the lens and damage the eye. Have a lens case ready.
Medical history, medicines, skin conditions around the eyes
Thin or inflamed skin, eczema or psoriasis near the eye, and some medicines mean extra care or no treatment.
Her natural colouring, face shape and what she wants
Guides the colour and the brow shape.
When she last had the treatment, and any home plucking or dyeing
Over-plucked brows need time to regrow; home dye may have used an unsafe product.

head: Prevents the treatment (refer to a doctor or pharmacist)
Restricts it (adapt, or avoid the area)
rows: Conjunctivitis: red, watering, sticky or gritty eyes
A stye
Cuts, sores, swelling or bruising around the eyes
Very red, watering or sore eyes for any reason
Skin infections near the eye, including cold sores, impetigo and ringworm
A positive skin test, or a known allergy to tint or adhesive
Recent eye surgery or laser treatment
Hay fever or a cold with streaming eyes on the day
Contact lenses: remove them first
Dry, sensitive skin or mild eczema near the brows: gentle products, no wax
Moles, warts or skin tags in the brow: do not tweeze or wax over them
Very thin, over-plucked brows: shape only strays and let them regrow
Sunburn on the forehead: no wax or threading
Retinoid creams or acne medicine: no waxing, as the skin can tear
Nervous client who cannot keep her eyes closed: no lash tint until she can

blocks.note: You are not a doctor. Explain kindly, without naming a disease, that you cannot treat the eye area today, and suggest she sees a doctor or pharmacist. Record what you saw and offer to rebook.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: Lash and brow tints contain dyes that can cause a strong allergic reaction, and the eye is the worst place for one. A **skin test** shows, before the treatment, whether the client's skin reacts to the product.

flow: Do it 24 to 48 hours before the tint, or as the maker states
Clean a small area behind the ear or in the crook of the elbow and dry it
Mix a little of the same tint and the same developer that will be used
Apply a small dab (about the size of a coin) and let it dry
Tell her to leave it alone for 24 to 48 hours, and to wash it off and call the salon at once if it itches, burns or swells
Record the date, time, the product and colour on the record card
Check the area when she returns, before you mix any tint

head: Result
What you see
What you do
rows: Negative
No change in the skin.
The tint can go ahead.
Positive
Redness, itching, swelling, burning, blisters or a rash at the test area.
Do **not** tint. Record it and advise her to see a pharmacist or doctor if it is still sore. Offer another treatment, such as a brow shape without tint.

ul: Test again if the client changes product or colour, has not been tinted for a long time, or if the maker says to test before every treatment. Many salons test every new client and repeat the test regularly, because allergies can develop at any time.
A skin test is also done for lash adhesive, by placing a small dot of adhesive behind the ear or on the inner arm, or a few individual lashes on the outer lashes, as the maker states.
Hair colour is also skin-tested in the same way: the test protects the client in every service that uses a dye.

blocks.note: No skin test means no tint. A client who says 'I have had it done before and I was fine' can still react today. Explain that the test protects her eyes, and book the test and the treatment together.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Check the record card: negative skin test, no contraindications, contact lenses out.

Lay the client back on the couch or a reclining chair with her head supported, so she is still and comfortable and you can see both eyes clearly. Put on a headband and protect her clothing with a towel.
Wash your hands; put on gloves if the maker or the Centre says so.
Remove eye make-up with a gentle, oil-free remover on damp cotton, and clean and dry the lashes and brows. Tint does not take well on oily lashes.
Lay out: a non-metallic dish, disposable tint brushes, barrier cream, eye shields or damp pads, cotton pads and buds, a bowl of clean water, a timer, tint stain remover and the lined, lidded bin.

flow: Apply a thin layer of petroleum jelly to the skin under the lower lashes and on the upper lid, close to the lashes but not on them
Ask her to look up; place a damp eye shield or pad under the lower lashes, snug against the lid
Ask her to close her eyes gently and keep them closed until you say
Mix the tint and developer in the non-metallic dish, as the maker says
With a disposable brush, apply the tint to the upper lashes from root to tip, on the top and the underside, and to the lower lashes
Keep the tint off the skin; wipe any slip at once with a damp cotton bud
Start the timer and stay with her
When the time is up, remove the shields and wipe with damp cotton pads, gently, until the pads come away clean
Check for stains and tint under the eye; only then may she open her eyes
Brush the brows into place with a clean spoolie
Apply barrier cream around (not on) the brows
Apply the tint from the outer end inwards, following the shape you want, with a thin even layer
Time it as the maker says: brows take colour fast, so often less time than the lashes
Wipe away the tint with damp cotton, from the outer end inwards; wipe one brow early if you want it lighter
Check both brows match; remove any skin stain with tint stain remover

blocks.note: The client keeps her eyes **closed** from the moment the first lash is tinted until the last pad comes away clean. Tell her to say if her eyes sting, and stop and rinse at once if they do. Never leave her alone with tint on.
blocks.label: Safety

head: Point
What to know
rows: Development time
Typically about 5 to 10 minutes for lashes and 1 to 3 minutes for brows, but **follow the maker's time**. Longer does not make a darker colour; it only irritates the skin and eyes.
Order of treatments
Tint before you shape. Tint stings freshly tweezed skin and stains the open follicles, and the tint colours the brow so you can see its full shape before you remove hairs.
A paler result than expected
Barrier cream on the hairs, oily lashes, old developer, or too short a time. Repeat only if the skin test was negative and the maker allows it.
Stains on the skin
Too little barrier cream or the shield slipped. Use tint stain remover on cotton, away from the eyes.
How long it lasts
About 4 to 6 weeks, as the lashes and brows shed and regrow.

blocks.note: Set the timer the moment the last lash is coated, and write the colour and time on the card. 'Black, lashes 8 minutes; dark brown, brows 2 minutes' lets the next therapist repeat the result, or lighten it.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Measuring, designing and shaping the brows

blocks.p: A good brow shape follows the client's bone structure and face shape and keeps the natural line. Measure first, mark, agree the shape with the client, and only then remove hair. Hair removed by mistake takes weeks to grow back.
Hold an orange stick or a brow pencil against the face as a straight line, with the client looking straight ahead, and mark each point lightly with a white pencil.

head: Point
Where the line runs
What it gives you
rows: 1. Start (inner end)
Straight up from the outer edge of the nostril, past the inner corner of the eye.
Where the brow should begin. Hairs between the brows, nearer the nose than this line, are removed.
2. Arch (highest point)
From the outer edge of the nostril through the outer edge of the iris (the coloured part of the eye) or the pupil.
Where the arch sits: usually about two-thirds of the way along the brow.
3. End (outer tail)
From the outer edge of the nostril past the outer corner of the eye.
Where the brow should finish. The tail should not drop lower than the start of the brow, or the eye looks sad.

head: Face shape
Brow that suits it
Why
rows: Round
A soft, higher arch, slightly angled
Adds length and lifts the face.
Square
A soft, curved arch; not too thin
Softens a strong jaw.
Long (oblong)
A flatter, straighter brow
Makes the face look shorter and wider.
Heart
A soft, rounded arch
Balances a wide forehead and narrow chin.
Oval
A gently curved, natural arch
Keeps the balance the face already has.

blocks.note: Keep the natural thickness where you can. Very thin brows are hard to regrow and look dated. Remove mostly from **underneath** and **between** the brows; take only obvious strays from above, because the top line gives the brow its shape.
blocks.label: Tip

flow: Wash your hands; use clean, disinfected or sterilised slanted tweezers
Clean the brow area with a mild antiseptic lotion on cotton and brush the hairs into place
Measure, mark and agree the shape
A warm, damp cotton pad on the brow for a minute softens the skin and opens the follicles
Stretch the skin gently between two fingers
Grip each hair close to the skin and pull it out quickly in the direction of growth
Work from underneath and between the brows, a few hairs at a time, alternating between the brows
Brush the brows and stand back often to check that both match
Wipe away loose hairs with damp cotton
Apply a soothing antiseptic lotion or a cool compress

ul: Pulling in the direction of growth lifts the hair out whole, with less pain, and is less likely to break it or leave an ingrown hair.
Stretching the skin lessens the pull and the pain, and stops the skin lifting.
Do not tweeze over moles, warts, spots, cuts or broken skin.
If a tiny blood spot appears, put on gloves, press with clean cotton and bin it in the lined bin.
Brow scissors can trim long hairs: brush them up, trim only the tips above the top line, and brush them back.

head: Method
How it works
Points
rows: Threading
A twisted loop of cotton thread is rolled over the skin and catches and lifts out rows of hairs from the root.
Quick and precise for whole rows; no heat or chemicals, so it suits skin that cannot be waxed. Needs practice. Fresh thread for every client. Can be sore, and the skin reddens for a short while.
Hot (hard) wax
Wax is applied warm, sets on the skin and is removed without a strip, gripping the short hairs.

Grips short, coarse hairs and is gentler on the thin skin around the eye than strip wax. Test the temperature on your inner wrist, then on a small patch of the client's skin. Apply with the growth, remove against it, skin held taut, away from the eye. Never over moles, thin or sore skin, or skin on retinoids.
Warm (strip) wax
A thin layer is removed with a strip.
Used by some salons for brows with great care; hot wax is usually preferred near the eye.

blocks.note: Tweezers, threading and waxing all remove the hair from the **root**, so they last about 4 to 6 weeks. Trimming with scissors only shortens the hair. A brow razor shaves at the surface and the hair returns within days; a used razor goes in the sharps box.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: False lashes are a temporary treatment for an occasion or a look. **Strip lashes** come as one band glued along the lash line and are removed the same day or the next. **Individual lashes** (small clusters or flares, or single lashes) are glued a few at a time onto the natural lashes and can last a few days to a couple of weeks with the right adhesive. Semi-permanent lash extensions, glued one by one to single lashes, are a separate skill with further training.

ul: Check for contraindications: no eye infections, sore or watering eyes, or allergy to the adhesive. Do a skin test for the adhesive as the maker states, especially for clients who have reacted before.
Some adhesives contain **latex**; a client with a latex allergy needs a latex-free adhesive, after a skin test.
Contact lenses: safest out during application, or as the client and the maker prefer.
Wash your hands. Clean the lashes and lids so they are free of oil and make-up: adhesive does not hold on oily lashes.

flow: Lift the strip from its case with clean tweezers
Measure it against the client's eye, from the inner corner to the outer corner
If it is too long, trim it from the outer end, a little at a time, with clean scissors
Bend the strip gently into a curve so it follows the lid
Apply a thin line of adhesive along the band
Wait a few seconds until the adhesive turns tacky (clear and sticky), so it holds at once
Ask her to look down; place the strip as close to the natural lash line as possible, centre first, then press the inner and outer corners into place
Hold for a few seconds; check both eyes match

ul: A strip that starts too close to the inner corner irritates the eye and feels heavy, which is why it is trimmed from the **outer** end.
Too much adhesive squeezes onto the lid and lashes, shows, and is hard to remove.
Keep adhesive and tweezers away from the eyeball; never apply with the eye wide open and looking up.

flow: Client looks down, eyes relaxed
Pick up a cluster or flare with tweezers by its tip
Dip the base in a small drop of adhesive
Lay it on top of the natural lashes, base at the lash line (not on the skin), starting at the outer corner
Work inwards, using shorter lengths towards the inner corner
Let the adhesive set before she opens her eyes fully; check both eyes match
Hold a cotton pad with lash adhesive remover (or the oil-based remover the maker gives) on the closed eye for a short while
Peel a strip lash gently from the outer corner inwards; lift individuals with a cotton bud or tweezers once the adhesive has softened
Clean the lash line with remover on a cotton bud
Never pull: it tears out the natural lashes and can damage the lid

ul: Do not rub the eyes, sleep face down or get the lashes wet for the time the adhesive maker says.
Avoid oil-based make-up removers near the lashes, which dissolve the adhesive.
Remove strip lashes before bed; clean and store them to reuse on the same client only.
Come back to have individuals removed, or remove them with a suitable remover; never pull them off.

blocks.h: Why hygiene matters so much here

blocks.p: The eye is easily infected, and eye infections such as conjunctivitis pass from client to client on fingers, brushes, pads and tweezers. Every tool and every pad is either single-use or cleaned and disinfected between clients.

head: Item
What you do
rows: Your hands
Wash before and after each client; gloves if the maker or Centre says so, and whenever there is blood.
Spoolies, disposable tint brushes, mascara wands, cotton pads and buds, orange sticks, eye shields, thread
One client only, then the lined, lidded bin.
Tweezers, brow scissors, lash applicators, metal combs
Remove hairs and product, wash in warm soapy water, rinse, dry, then disinfect for the full time the maker gives, or sterilise in an autoclave. Store clean and covered.
Tint dishes and measuring tools
Wash and disinfect after each use.
Mixed tint and used wax
Thrown away, never reused.
Creams and barrier products
Taken from the jar with a clean spatula; lids closed.
Towels and headbands
Fresh for every client; used ones into the closed laundry bin.
Blades (brow razors)
The sharps box.
The couch, chair, magnifying lamp and trolley
Wiped with disinfectant between clients; fresh couch roll.

head: Contra-action
What you see
What you do
rows: Tint or developer in the eye
Stinging, watering, redness; the client blinks or opens her eyes.

Stop. Remove the shields and tint from the lashes with damp pads, then rinse the eye at once with plenty of clean, cool water or sterile **eye wash**, tilting the head so the water runs away from the other eye, for several minutes. Advise medical help if it stays red or sore. Record it.
Allergic reaction to tint
Redness, itching, swelling of the lids, watering, a rash, sometimes hours later.
Stop; remove the product with cool water; apply a cool compress; advise a doctor. Record the product. She must not be tinted again.
Tint stain on the skin
Dark marks around the brow or under the eye.
Tint stain remover on cotton, kept away from the eye. Prevent it with barrier cream and a snug shield.
Redness and slight swelling after tweezing, threading or waxing
Pink skin and small bumps around the follicles.
Normal and short-lived: soothing antiseptic lotion and a cool compress.
Blood spots after tweezing
Tiny spots at the follicles.
Gloves on; press with clean cotton; bin it; soothing antiseptic.
Skin lifted or burnt by wax
Raw, shiny or red patch.
Cool it under cool running water; soothing antiseptic; no make-up; record it; advise a doctor if it blisters.
Adhesive irritating the eye
Stinging, watering, red lid.
Remove the lash gently with remover; rinse the eye; cool compress.
Ingrown hairs or folliculitis after tweezing
Spots in the brow days later.
Advise gentle exfoliation and no picking; refer if infected.

blocks.note: Rinsing an eye: use the sterile eye wash from the first aid kit, or clean cool running water, for at least 10 minutes if a chemical is in the eye. Hold the lids open and keep the water flowing from the inner corner outwards. Never put developer, remover or 'neutraliser' in an eye.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.note: Record every contra-action on the record card and tell your supervisor, so that the product is not used on her again and the Centre can learn from it.
blocks.label: Remember

head: After
Advice
Why
rows: A lash tint
Do not rub the eyes
Remove eye make-up gently with a mild, oil-free remover
Contact the salon at once if the eyes become red, itchy, swollen or sore
Protects the eye and keeps the colour; a late reaction needs quick attention.
A brow tint
Avoid harsh scrubs, strong cleansers and oily products on the brows
Use sunscreen; strong sun fades the colour
Keeps the colour longer.
Brow shaping (tweezing, threading, waxing)
No make-up, creams, perfume, touching, strong sun, sea bathing or heat on the area for about 24 hours
Cool compress if it feels sore
Do not pluck the regrowth at home; book a tidy-up in a few weeks
Gentle exfoliation after a few days to prevent ingrown hairs
The follicles are open and germs can enter; home plucking spoils the shape.
False lashes
Do not rub or pull; keep them dry for the time the adhesive maker says
Remove with a suitable remover, never by pulling
Protects the natural lashes.

blocks.p: Suggest when she should come back: a tint usually about every 4 to 6 weeks, and a brow tidy every few weeks. A new skin test is needed if the maker or the Centre's rules say so.

head: What to record
Example
rows: Date, client's details, signature
07/11/2026, Marcia Reid, Yallahs; signed
Skin test
Tested 05/11/2026, 4:15 p.m., behind the ear, black tint + maker's developer; checked 07/11: negative
Contraindications and checks
None; contact lenses removed
Treatment, products, colours and timing
Lashes: black, 8 minutes. Brows: dark brown, 2 minutes. Brows shaped with tweezers; soothing lotion applied
Reactions
Slight redness after tweezing, settled before she left
Advice given and next visit
Aftercare sheet given; rebook in 5 weeks
Therapist
Trainee's name, checked by the instructor

blocks.note: Record cards are personal information. Under Jamaica's Data Protection Act they must be kept private and secure, and they are the evidence that a skin test was done if a client later has a reaction.
blocks.label: Jamaica

flow: Throw away leftover tint, single-use brushes, pads and shields
Wash and disinfect the tint dish
Clean, then disinfect or sterilise tweezers and scissors
Wipe the couch, lamp and trolley; fresh couch roll
Towels and headband into the laundry bin
Close and wipe the products; store them cool and dark
Wash your hands

ul: I can describe the eye area, the lash and brow hairs and their growth cycle, and say why a tint lasts about 4 to 6 weeks.
I can name the tint products and say what the developer does, and why hair colour for the head is never used near the eyes.
I can mix, store and dispose of tint and developer safely.
I can carry out a consultation and explain why I ask about allergies, eye surgery and contact lenses.
I can name the contraindications that prevent a treatment and those that restrict it, and refer a client kindly.
I can carry out, record and read a skin test, and I never tint after a positive result or without a test.
I can choose a tint colour that suits the client's hair colour and skin tone.
I can protect the skin and eye, apply, time and remove a lash tint and a brow tint, and explain why tinting comes before shaping.
I can measure a brow with the three-point guide and plan a shape for the client's face.
I can shape brows with tweezers in the direction of growth, keeping both brows even, and explain how threading and hot wax are used.
I can measure, trim, apply and remove strip lashes, and apply individual lashes.
I can keep the treatment hygienic and say which items are single-use and how tools are disinfected or sterilised.
I can deal with tint in the eye, an allergic reaction, stains, redness and blood spots.
I can give aftercare advice and fill in the record card.

blocks.note: In essay answers, give the reason for each step. For example: 'I place a damp shield under the lower lashes and ask her to close her eyes, so that tint cannot run into the eye or stain the skin.'
blocks.label: Tip

terms: Conjunctivitis
An infection or irritation of the membrane over the eye; red, watering, gritty eyes ('pink eye'); very contagious.
Stye
An infected lash follicle or gland at the edge of the eyelid.
Follicle
The small pocket in the skin from which a hair grows.
Anagen
The growing stage of the hair cycle.
Catagen
The short changing stage, when the hair stops growing.
Telogen
The resting stage, before the hair falls out.
Tint
A permanent dye made for lashes and brows.
Developer
The weak hydrogen peroxide that starts the colour reaction.
Hydrogen peroxide
The chemical in the developer; weakened by heat and light.
Non-metallic dish
A plastic or glass dish for mixing tint; metal can react with peroxide.
Barrier cream
Petroleum jelly or similar, applied to the skin to stop staining.
Eye shield
A paper shield or damp pad placed under the lower lashes.
Skin test (patch test)
A small test of the product on the skin, 24 to 48 hours before, to check for allergy.
Positive reaction
Redness, itching, swelling or blisters at the skin test: do not treat.
Contraindication
Something that prevents a treatment or means it must be changed.
Contra-action
An unwanted reaction during or after a treatment.
Eye wash
Sterile liquid in the first aid kit for rinsing an eye.
Tint stain remover
A product that lifts tint from the skin; kept away from the eyes.
Spoolie
A disposable brush for brushing lashes and brows.
Three-point guide
The start, arch and end lines used to measure a brow.
Arch
The highest point of the brow.
Tweezers
The tool that removes hairs one at a time; slanted tips are usual for brows.
Direction of growth
The way the hair lies; tweeze and apply wax with it, and remove wax against it.
Threading
Removing rows of hairs from the root with a twisted cotton thread.
Hot (hard) wax
Wax that sets on the skin and is removed without a strip; gentle near the eye.
Strip lashes
False lashes on one band, glued along the lash line.
Individual lashes
Small clusters or single false lashes glued a few at a time.
Latex-free adhesive
Lash adhesive for clients allergic to latex.
Tacky
Adhesive that has become sticky and ready to hold.
Single-use (disposable)
Used on one client and then thrown away.
Sterilise
Kill all germs and spores, for example in an autoclave.
Sharps box
A rigid container for used razors and blades.
Record card
The client's record of checks, skin tests, treatments, colours, timings, reactions and advice.

c1.title: A graduation in Mona
c1.text: Abigail Scott, 22, books a lash and brow tint for her graduation at the university in Mona in three days. She has never had a tint before. She says she dyes her hair at home 'all the time with no problem' and asks trainee Nickesha to skip the skin test and tint her today, because she is busy. She wears contact lenses and has dark brown hair and a deep skin tone.

c2.title: Tint day in the Port Antonio training salon
c2.text: In the Centre's salon in Port Antonio, trainee Jada is tinting her partner Shevelle's lashes. She mixes the tint in a small metal bowl from the kitchen. She covers the lower lashes thickly with petroleum jelly before placing the shield. Halfway through the timed development, Shevelle says her left eye is stinging and starts to blink. The maker's leaflet says 10 minutes for lashes; Jada had planned 20 minutes 'for a really dark result'.

c3.title: A brow rescue in Brown's Town
c3.text: Mrs. Yvonne Palmer, 45, comes to a salon in Brown's Town. She has been plucking her own brows for years; they are thin, with a wide gap between them and tails that drop below the inner ends. She has a round face. A small mole sits inside the left brow, and she has a sore, red lump on the edge of her right lower eyelid that appeared yesterday. She wants a brow shape and a lash tint.

c4.title: Carnival lashes in Kingston
c4.text: Danielle Morgan, 27, wants dramatic strip lashes for a carnival band fete in Kingston. She tells trainee Ricardo that a plaster once gave her a red, itchy rash, and that she is 'sure it was the rubber'. Ricardo's first strip is longer than her eye. After the fete, Danielle's friend pulls the strips straight off, and several of Danielle's own lashes come out with them.

c5.title: A hot stock cupboard in Falmouth
c5.text: At a salon in Falmouth, the lash tints and developer are kept on an open shelf beside a window that gets the afternoon sun, next to the wax heater. The last three brow tints at the salon came out much paler than expected. After a client's brow tint, trainee Omar sees a dark stain on the skin above her brow, and leftover mixed tint sits in the dish, which he plans to cover and keep for the next client.

questions.q: How should Nickesha answer Abigail's request to skip the skin test?
o: Agree, since a client who dyes her hair safely cannot react to tint
Explain that a skin test is still needed, and book it first
Agree, but tint only the brows, since they are not near the eye
Tint her today, but use half the developer to make it gentler
questions.why: A test is needed before a tint, as the maker states: a dye allergy can start at any time, and a reaction at the eye is serious. Home hair dye proves nothing about this product. Book the test now and the tint 24 to 48 hours later.

questions.q: Which colour choice is most likely to suit Abigail?
o: Light brown lashes and grey brows
Black lashes and dark brown or black brows
Grey lashes and light brown brows
Blue-black brows and light brown lashes
questions.why: Lashes take the darkest colour so they look longer and thicker, and brows are tinted close to the hair colour; dark brown or black suits dark brown hair and a deep skin tone. Grey and light brown are for fair or grey hair.

questions.q: What must happen about Abigail's contact lenses on the day of the tint?
o: She takes them out before the tint and keeps them in a case
She keeps them in, so the tint cannot reach the eye surface
She wears them, but Nickesha tints only the upper lashes
She removes one lens, so she can still see with the other eye
questions.why: Tint or water can get behind a lens and damage the eye, and a lens can hold a chemical against the eye. Lenses come out before any tint, and go back in only after the eyes are clean.

questions.q: What is wrong with the bowl Jada mixed the tint in?
o: Metal keeps the tint too cold to develop fully
Metal can react with the peroxide developer
A kitchen bowl is too wide for the small amount
Metal bowls make the tint develop far too fast
questions.why: Tint is mixed in a clean, non-metallic dish because metal can react with the hydrogen peroxide developer. A bowl from the kitchen also breaks the rule that food items and salon chemicals stay apart.

questions.q: Why will Shevelle's lower lashes most likely come out pale?
o: Lower lashes cannot take tint, whatever is done to them
The shield pressed against them stops the colour taking
The thick petroleum jelly on the lashes blocked the tint
The metal bowl weakened the tint before it was applied
questions.why: Barrier cream goes on the skin only. Tint cannot take through petroleum jelly, so any that reaches the hairs leaves them pale. Apply it thinly, close to the lashes but not on them.

questions.q: Shevelle's eye is stinging. What should Jada do first?
o: Tell her to keep her eyes shut tight until the timer finishes
Add a little developer to the eye to neutralise the tint
Wipe the tint away and rinse the eye with cool water or eye wash
Dab the stinging eye with a dry tissue and carry on timing
questions.why: Stinging means tint has reached the eye. Stop, wipe the tint away with damp pads, then rinse the eye with plenty of clean cool water or sterile eye wash, and get medical help if it stays sore. Never put developer in an eye.

questions.q: What is the result of leaving the lash tint on for 20 minutes instead of the maker's 10?
o: A much darker colour that lasts twice as long
The same colour, with more risk of irritation
The colour reverses and the lashes turn lighter
The tint sets hard and must be filed off the lashes
questions.why: The colour develops within the maker's time; extra time does not deepen it, but it keeps a chemical on the thin skin and near the eye for longer, which can irritate both. Follow the maker's time.

questions.q: What should the therapist do about the red lump on Mrs. Palmer's lower eyelid?
o: Tint the lashes but cover the lump with barrier cream
Postpone the lash tint and suggest she sees a doctor
Press the lump with a hot compress until it bursts, then tint
Tint only the right eye's upper lashes, well away from the lump
questions.why: A sore red lump on the lid edge is likely a stye, an infection that prevents any treatment near that eye. Refer her kindly without naming it, and rebook the tint once it has healed.

questions.q: Which brow shape should the therapist plan for Mrs. Palmer?
o: A thin, flat line with the tails dropping lower still
A fuller brow with a soft, higher arch and the tails lifted level
A very short brow ending above the centre of each eye
A heavy, straight brow drawn well into the gap
questions.why: A round face suits a soft, higher arch, and tails that drop below the brow's start make the eyes look sad. Over-plucked brows need to regrow, so remove only strays and let the thickness come back.

questions.q: How should the therapist deal with the mole inside the left brow?
o: Tweeze the hairs on and around it like the rest of the brow
Wax over it, since wax removes hairs on a mole more gently
Leave it alone and shape the hairs around it carefully
Trim the mole flat with the brow scissors before tweezing
questions.why: Never tweeze or wax over a mole, wart or skin tag: it can be torn and bleed. Work around it. If hairs grow from it, leave them or trim them, and refer any changing mole to a doctor.

questions.q: Mrs. Palmer's brows still have a wide gap between them. Where does the inner end of each brow belong?
o: Straight up from the nostril's edge, past the inner eye corner
On a line from the nostril through the outer edge of the iris
On a line from the nostril past the outer corner of the eye
Straight up from the centre of the pupil as she looks ahead
questions.why: The first of the three points is the start: a line straight up from the outer edge of the nostril, passing the inner corner of the eye. The line through the iris gives the arch, and the one past the outer corner gives the end.

questions.q: What should Ricardo do about Danielle's reaction to the plaster?
o: Use the usual adhesive, but apply only a very thin line of it
Choose a latex-free adhesive and test it first, as the maker states
Refuse the strip lashes, since any adhesive will cause a rash
Use the usual adhesive and give her a cool compress afterwards
questions.why: A rash from a plaster suggests a latex allergy, and many lash adhesives contain latex. A latex-free adhesive, skin-tested first, keeps the eye area safe.

questions.q: Ricardo's strip is longer than Danielle's eye. What should he do?
o: Apply it as it is, pressing the extra past the outer corner
Trim it from the inner end so it sits away from the nose
Trim it from the outer end, a little at a time, to fit
Cut it into two halves and apply them side by side
questions.why: A strip is measured against the eye and trimmed from the outer end. A strip that runs into the inner corner feels heavy and irritates the eye; one that runs past the outer corner lifts and pulls.

questions.q: Why did Danielle lose her own lashes when the strips were pulled off?
o: The adhesive was still bonded to her own lashes
Strip lashes always take some natural lashes with them when removed
The carnival lashes were too heavy and had pulled the follicles loose
Her natural lashes were already shedding because of the adhesive
questions.why: Strips are removed only after the adhesive has been softened with remover, then peeled gently from the outer corner. Pulling a set strip tears the natural lashes out with it.

questions.q: What is the most likely reason the salon's brow tints have come out pale?
o: The sun and heat have weakened the developer
The salon's clients all have very coarse brow hair
Brow tint should always be mixed with two developers
The wax heater's fumes have bleached the tint
questions.why: Hydrogen peroxide developer breaks down in heat and light and loses its strength, so the colour does not develop. Tints and developer are stored in a cool, dark, dry cupboard with the lids tight.

questions.q: How should Omar remove the stain above the client's brow?
o: Rub it with a cotton pad soaked in nail polish remover
Use tint stain remover on cotton, well away from the eye
Leave it, as it will become part of the brow shape
Scrub it with the spoolie and plenty of warm, soapy water
questions.why: Tint stain remover is made for skin and lifts the dye; it is used away from the eyes. Next time, apply barrier cream around the brow and work neatly. Polish remover and scrubbing would irritate the thin skin.

questions.q: What should happen to the leftover mixed tint in the dish?
o: Cover it and keep it for the next client, as Omar plans
Pour it back into the tint tube to stop waste
Throw it away, and wash and disinfect the dish
Keep it in the fridge for up to a week
questions.why: Once tint and developer are mixed, the reaction has started and the mix cannot be kept or reused. Mix only what you need, bin the rest, and wash and disinfect the dish.

questions.q: A client is booked for a brow tint and a brow shape in the same visit. Why is the tint done first?
o: Tint on freshly tweezed skin stings and stains the open follicles
The tint must soak into the open follicles to colour the roots
Tweezing after a tint makes the hairs grow back a lighter colour
The shaping must be last so that the tint has time to dry on the hairs
questions.why: Tweezing or waxing leaves the follicles open and the skin tender, so tint applied afterwards stings and stains. Tinting first also shows the full brow so the shape is easier to see.

questions.q: Why do tweezed brow hairs grow back after a few weeks?
o: The hair is removed at the surface, so the root is untouched
Tweezing only lightens the hair and does not remove it
The follicle stays alive and grows a new hair
Brow hairs are joined in pairs, so one always remains
questions.why: Tweezing removes the hair from the root, but the follicle remains and produces a new hair as the cycle continues (anagen, catagen, telogen), usually within about 4 to 6 weeks.

questions.q: Why do you brush the brows into place and clean the skin with a mild antiseptic before you start to tweeze?
o: To see how the hairs lie and to cut down germs
To make the hairs stand up so that they snap off more easily
To numb the skin so that the client cannot feel the tweezers
To stop the follicles from closing before the hairs are pulled
questions.why: Brushing shows the natural direction and shape of the brow, which you tweeze with. Cleaning the skin cuts down the germs that could enter the follicles once hairs are pulled out.
